utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. May I take this opportunity once again to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Strinovic. At the end of your -- at the end of our day yesterday, you were discussing the updated materials that you prepared for us. Now I'm going to move away from that. I'm going to ask you some particular questions about particular locations, and in connection with that I'll show you a video and then a little later on a few documents.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, I'd ask that we switch to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for this, Your Honours, I believe it's best to push the computer evidence button. I'm just going a little slow to make sure everything's in order. Do we need to -- we can take a moment if we need to, to make sure everyone's got the proper computer screen on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are we looking for? I'm sorry, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In a moment I'm going to play a video. I was just waiting because they looked like they need the proper screen to show it. Now with the assistance of Ms. Walpita, if we can show a clip from Exhibit -- this is from Exhibit 318, Your Honours, which was admitted into evidence yesterday and this clip relates to exhumation and examination of bodies at Bacin. If we could see the video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, just for the record was that who speak with the interviewer in the first part of that clip?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you yourself participate in the examination of bodies exhumed from Bacin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This video's fairly brief, but does it accurately reflect the work done on the bodies that were exhumed from Bacin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. It does give you a picture of what we do and how when we are dealing with the case of a mass grave site like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's all the video I'll ask you to watch today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At this point with the assistance of the usher, Your Honours, I'd like to hand the witness a binder of documents, and I also have copies for Your Honours. These are 55 documents. I don't intend to ask the witness about each one, although he has had a chance to review them, and I'll discuss this with the witness. Yes, one copy for the witness, please. And a gave a copy to the Defence yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, while we're passing out the other binders, if you could just take a moment to look through the index there, look through the documents, and just familiarise yourself with them, please. Dr. Strinovic, did you review these materials on Monday here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What kind of documents are these for the most part?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that they are practical examples of autopsy reports, as we call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How do these documents relate, if at all, to the information contained in your updated list that you've provided and that you discussed with us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain your question a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Of course. Let me try to put it more clearly. Do the documents in this binder -- are they related in any way to the information that's included in the updated materials that you provided to the Prosecution, the documents that we talked about yesterday in court?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because for certain cases, namely those cases for which the institute for forensic medicine in Zagreb did not perform the autopsies, and these are precisely these cases, we received certain materials in order to be able to answer your questions and to be able to send you the material that we did. So we had to review those protocols and specifically the cause of death listed in them to find what was relevant for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you look in particular at the first 45 documents, and they're all tabbed, you'll see that 1 through 45 purport to be prepared and signed by Josip Dujella. Who is Josip Dujella.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Josip Dujella has been a pathologist at the general hopped in Zadar for a long time, and as such he did not perform only autopsies as a pathologist, because else's a pathologist, but he has also appeared before courts as a forensic expert and performed autopsies in Zadar and the surrounding area. So Dr. Dujella did not have an official paper, a diploma as a forensic expert but has worked as an expert, as an experienced doctor, for many years and has performed autopsies and identifications during the Homeland War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was he capable of performing these kind of examinations under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, Dr. Dujella has without any doubt been capable of performing those autopsies because he had done many of them before the war. He has great experience in writing autopsy reports and is perfectly qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As I said I'm not going to ask you to look at each you have the documents in this binder but I'm going to ask you to look at nine or 10 particular ones. First, if you could please turn to tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter Exhibit number 1008. Perhaps it could also be brought up on the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an autopsy report, that is findings after autopsy, signed by Josip Dujella regarding Stana Vickovic which was found in Skabrnja. From the protocol, from the autopsy report we see that a gunshot wound was found on the head, and what is noteworthy here is that this gunshot wound, one centimetre in size, that has another indication of a gunshot injury has also signs of burn on one of the sleeves. Such a wound also indicates the distance from the weapon at the time of firing. Let me clarify. On the basis of the appearance of a gunshot wound, we can determine whether it was inflicted from a distance or from a relative proximity. If the mouth of the gun is on the skin or just a few centimetres from the skin, we speak about blank-point range. Relative distance is when the gun was a bit further away and we find a particular tattoo mark on the skin resulting from such a wound and also burn signs. If the distance was greater, then there are no other traces on the skin other than the hole made by the bullet itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for not mentioning this in advance. The way the binder is structured is that there's a B/C/S version and the English is right behind it. You probably discovered that on your own by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Doctor, you may have covered this in your answer, but just to be sure, specifically in regards to Stana Vickovic does it indicate the distance from which that gunshot to the head was inflicted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not explicitly, but from the description that is given in the autopsy report, it follows that the gunshot wound was inflicted from the so-called relative distance, from what we call relative distance -- relative proximity. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. And Your Honours, I would just mention that Stana Vickovic was mentioned in the testimony of Neven Segaric. The same is true, in fact, of the names that appear in the next three documents. Doctor, could we turn to tab 27, these.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request would it be possible for us to have a copy or at least to show the English version on Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The interpreters have requested a copy of this or to see the English on Sanction. I'm afraid I don't have another copy of the binder, but could we perhaps put the English version on Sanction? Is that agreeable to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. What is Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is on the e-court is what -- well, I don't -- sorry, I misunderstood the interpreter's request. It's not possible to put this on Sanction. We don't have the documents prepared for that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: E-court, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: E-court. I'm having a conversation with the interpreters, Dr. Strinovic. I'm sorry if that's confusing. If we might put the English version on e-court, Your Honour, that might assist the interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Tab 27 is 65 ter number 1014. If we could go ahead and turn to that. Dr. Strinovic, what is this document behind tab 27, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is an autopsy report for Krsto Segaric. The age is not visible from this copy. We see reference of an entry gunshot wound one centimetre in size on the left cheek, and there is a similar injury on the chin below the left half of the lower lip. In both cases with both entry gunshot wounds there is reference to burn rings from which it follows that they were inflicted from relative proximity. So there are two gunshot entry wounds on the cheek and below the chin -- on the chin that are consistent with firing from relative proximity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Let's turn now to tab 33. This is 65 ter Exhibit number 1020. Doctor, when you've had a chance to look over that, please tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is yet another autopsy report concerning Grgica Segaric, age 80, also from Skabrnja. It is said that on the left side of the thorax there are two entry gunshot wounds, one above the other, each sized 9 by 5 millimetres or so, and there is a ring around them 3 to six millimetres wide. So we have two gunshot wounds on the chest. And in view of their appearance, they are consistent with firing from a distance. Also, we see that there is an entry and exit wound on another part of the body, on the lower arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. One final document with regard to Skabrnja victims. Please look at tab 41, which is 65 ter Exhibit number 1028.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another autopsy report concerning Ante Razov, age 36. There is a reference to an injury of the left earlobe that was cut off by a sharp object, then an injury on the right cheek in the form of an entry gunshot wound, star shaped, two and a half centimetres in size, and the exit was on the back of the head on the left side. In view of the characteristics of the entry wound, it was inflicted from point-blank range. So the mouth of the gun was leaning on the left cheek at the time when it fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you perhaps just read out the last three sentences of Dr. Dujella's opinion at the end of this document, please? It begins with, "The injuries inflicted with ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if it's of any assistance to the ushers, it would be on the second page of the B/C/S and the final page of the English. Excuse me, on the third page of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you want me to read the last three sentences, "in the opinion of Mr. Dujella"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct. It begins with the words, "The injuries inflicted with." If you have trouble finding it, please let me know and I can help you more precisely.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the sentence that begins with, "The gunshot wound to the head was inflicted from point-blank range, and the gunshot canal goes from the left cheek to the back of the head. On its way there is the brain destroyed. The cervical -- on its path out, the contused and heavily damaged parts of the cerebrum, cerebellum, the pons, and the medulla. The injuries inflicted with cold arms evidently preceded the ultimate fatal entry-exit wound in the head. The wounds were not inflicted at the same time but in the course of a certain period of time and by several criminals. Their aim walls not only the deprivation of life but first, the prolonged subjection to physical and mental torture and the humiliation of a helpless, innocent victim."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, and my thanks to the ushers for getting the English version up there which helped the interpreters ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I believe there needs to be a correction to the record. Well, I'd like to ask for clarification. Should it read "the bullet canal runs from the right cheek towards the left cheek and backwards to the left occipital area"? I believe it mentions the left cheek, running from the left cheek, whereas it -- should it be the right cheek towards the left cheek and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We see a reference here. The gunshot wound to the head was at point-blank range and the bullet canal runs from the right check towards the left and backwards to the left occipital region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I'll now turn to victims from Bruska. And here, Your Honours, I would simply recall the testimony of Ante Marinovic and Jasna Denona. Doctor, if you could look at tab 46. This is 65 ter Exhibit number 1120. Tab 46, Your Honour -- or Dr. Strinovic, please. Doctor, this document is a little longer than the ones we've been looking at before, so please take a minute to familiarise yourself with this document and then when you're done, please first tell us what kind of document it is. Dr. Strinovic, before we get to the substance of this document, could you first tell us what kind of document it is, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is once again a record which was obviously compiled at the request of the court in -- county court in Zadar on site, and they are records taken down on the basis of three autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you look at the first page in B/C/S, and it appears on the second page in the English translation, who was the forensic expert involved in this on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Josip Dujella.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What are the names of the victims addressed in this document [Dujella]?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Marinovic, Krsto Marinovic, and Draginja Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does the document indicate the causes of death of those three victims? Perhaps we could start with Petar Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this -- this discussion of Petar Marinovic begins at page 3 of the English version and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For each of the above-listed persons, we have a description which indicates the cause of death. So with Petar Marinovic, for example, it says that on the clothing damages were found two centimetres in size, four damages, and also injuries on the right-hand side of the chest, the right side of the abdomen, and on the skeleton fractures of the lower jaw, fracture on the left upper leg, and the soft tissue was present only on the back and legs, the back portions of the body. And if we compare these injuries to the slashes on the clothing with the injuries on the skin of the back which were about six millimetres in diameter and round in shape, one arrives at the conclusion that they were gunshot wounds to the back. The exit wound was on the back -- entrance wound on the back, sorry, and the channel runs towards the front. Is that sufficient? May we move on to the next case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, please. Let's move to Krsto Marinovic. The discussion begins on page 6 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can Krsto Marinovic, there are multiple fractures of the bones of the head, the skull, and multiple fractures especially on the left half the skull, at the base of the skull in particular, and on the left upper side of the jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I could just interject. This is found at page 8 of the English, just to help the ushers follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please continue, Dr. Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Fractures were also found on the upper part of the left upper arm and also on the sleeve at the same point. There was a fracture of one of the pelvic bones and vertebra and right lower leg with holes on the clothes. So there was a fracture to the second lumbar vertebra, also under the hole in the clothes, also already described, and a multiple fracture of both bones of the right lower leg. And these holes on the clothes and fractures on the bone indicate that they were multiple gunshot wounds that caused this damage. And the third person is Draginja Marinovic, the last case. It is a woman. On her clothes in front holes were found up to one and a half centimetres on the left-hand side. So that was one hole, one tear, and two holes on the right sleeve. Also in the area of the 'kombine,' the left upper leg, and underneath there were holes to the clothing and multiple fractures of the right elbow bone, both bones of the right lower arm, a fracture of the upper leg underneath the hole to her clothing, and a fracture of the fourth vertebra and rib. On the back of her clothing holes of one centimetre diameter. These findings, and by comparing the defects to the clothing and the injuries to the body indicates that these were gunshot wounds that occurred from hand weapons, hand-held weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I think that's sufficient for this document. Could you please turn to the next tab, tab 47, and essentially go through the same exercise? And I think maybe even a little less detailed would be sufficient. If you can just focus on the conclusion as to cause of death, please. This is 65 ter Exhibit number 1123.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again this is a report from the on-site investigation conducted by the county court in Zadar. Dr. Dujella conducted the autopsy for Dusan Marinovic and Roko Marinovic. With Dusan Marinovic it is stated that on the basis of the appearance and size of the damage to the clothing and the injuries themselves that this was a case of gunshot wounds. With Roko Marinovic, once again by comparing the damages and the injury, it emerges that they were gunshot wounds, entrance-exit wounds to the chest, the thorax. That would briefly be a summary of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I think that's all for Bruska. Now I would ask you to look at tab 52 Your Honours this is 65 ter Exhibit number 1177.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, through an oversight on our part -- my part essentially, we don't have an English translation of this document yet. It has been requested, and what I would propose is just ask the witness a few questions about the B/C/S version. When the English translation comes, of course, we'll put it in e-court with the rest of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, again just have a moment to look through this, and when you're ready tell us what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report of an on-site investigation on the 12th 13th and 14th of June 1996 conducted by the county court in Karlovac. Present were forensic medical physicians Cadez, Gusic, and Balicevic. The place was Lipovacka-Dreznicka near Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question. Do you know those forensic medical physicians? Are you familiar with those people?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Cadez and Gusic have been working with me for a series of years and Dr. Drinko Balicevic is a pathologist from the hospital in Zagreb, and for five years, from 1995, he was the individual who attended most of the exhumations. And when the need arose he helped with the autopsies themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I won't ask you to address any specific individual here, but just looking through the document does it address causes of death as well as identification of the victims from Lipovaca.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both identification and causes of death for each of the cases studied, each person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think at this point we can turn to the next tab, which is tab 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we -- when we assembled these binders, we actually ran out of tabs at the end, so I hope it's not too confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, it's the next document, and it has handwritten "Poljanak-Vukovici" at the top. Are you able to find that document? It's 65 ter Exhibit number 1180.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, this one does have an English translation if you'd like to follow along. Again, the questions will be general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, take a moment to look at it and again please tell us what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is record, on-site investigation conducted by the county court in Zadar, and in attendance were forensic specialist Dr. Drazen Cuculic who conducted the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are addressed in this document, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a settlement called Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And again I won't ask you to look at any -- to discuss any particular individuals, but does this document address causes of death of -- of those victims?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report states the injuries and then the opinion given, identification, and cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour will certainly have noticed I haven't asked to admit these documents into evidence one by one as I've gone through them. What I would propose, Your Honour -- well, let me ask a few more questions and then I'll get to the issue of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I haven't asked you about every document in the binder here in court, but did you have an opportunity on Monday to review the entire binder?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do all of the documents contained in this binder include information that relates to the causes of death of the victims from the various locations addressed in -- in this case and in the updated materials that you provided?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And based on your review of the documents in this binder, do you believe these documents to be authentic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, then at this stage I what I would ask is that all of the documents in this binder be admitted into evidence. They are all in the e-court, and what I would suggest is that I have extra copies of the index that is at the beginning of this binder, and I would just -- I think the most practical solution would be if they are admitted is I could give an index to the court officer who could assign numbers after court rather than taking up court time to do that, but I leave to Your Honours, the procedure you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand what is it you're asking for. When you say the court officer would assign numbers outside court hours, is he going to assign numbers to each one of these reports, or is he going to give a number to the entire binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, either way is certainly fine with the Prosecution. As I understand it, these documents, each individual tab has been uploaded into e-court as a separate document. So the easiest thing might be to give them individual exhibit numbers. We would be fine with the binder receiving a number but think that would be easiest for the court officer, Your Honour, to have a number for each document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the court officer nods. I'm not quite sure what he's nodding to. But anyway, any objection, Mr. Milovancevic? Thank you very much. Then the documents in this binder are admitted into evidence, and may they please be given an exhibit number if it is possible to give it now quickly. If it is required that various numbers be given which may take court time, the court officer is asked to please do that outside court time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The exhibit numbers will be assigned outside of court time so as not to take up any time in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Perhaps now while I'm thinking of it with the assistance of the usher I would just pass an index to the court officer to make that easier later. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, thank you. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good day to you. My name -- or, rather, I'm Defence counsel for Milan Martic, and I'm going to ask you a few questions linked to your testimony here. When we're talking about a document relating -- or, rather, the document relating to the exhumation conducted in Vukovici, and that was conducted on the 13th of August, 1996, was on the 7th of November, 1991, the B/C/S number is 04693958. Do you have the document in front you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the list we have 10 individuals of which two were identified. Isn't that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this document it says, and you confirmed this, that at the institute the body remains were investigated belonging to at least three individuals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people from this list of 10 is on the list of those killed and how many on the list of missing persons or are they all on one list?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they're all on one list, but the fact is that of the 10 individuals, only two were identified by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that they're all on one list, can you tell us which list you have in mind, the list of killed, dead, or the list of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the list of missing persons that I was provided by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to move on to another document relating to Lipovacka-Dreznicka, and it says that the person went missing on the 28th of October 1991, and that the exhumation took place in 1996, and it was 046939591. That is the B/C/S number. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On this list of the seven persons, all seven were identified. The person under number 5, Brozincevic Mirko is the name, it says that the cause of death was a gunshot wound. Isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answer to a question from my colleague of the Prosecution, you said that there were no visible traces which would indicate the cause of death and that eyewitnesses had said that the wound was a gunshot entrance wound to the neck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In a situation of this kind, is it right for the forensic physician to say that the cause of death was gunshot wound or probably a gunshot wound or a third option? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a forensic physician, I can say that I would -- in my case I would say probably or most probably a gunshot wound. I wouldn't say that it was a gunshot wound as a certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly again that in this item 5, which refers to Mirko Brozincevic, it should be possibly or probably a gunshot wound as a cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the document relating to persons gone missing in Bacin, that's a list of 108 persons, and at the bottom of this document which is several pages long, you stated that 49 persons were autopsied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 49 or 48? The English version says 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a document in front of me in B/C/S which says at the last page, 108 missing in total, autopsied 49. So we will remind the Professor with the following question:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said there were 49 persons from this list and 44 from other -- plus 5. You said 44 from this list and 5 from other locations. That would make 49. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance, Your Honour, I can confirm that it does say 49 which is the original, so it appears to be a type open in the English translation. It should be number 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. It just says 48 bodies were processed, but if you add up the numbers there under cause of death it comes to 49. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday responding to a question from the Prosecution, you said that there remained 14 persons unidentified, out of which seven with gunshot wounds, seven with unknown cause of death. And you said you didn't know who these persons were. When you say you don't know who they are, do you mean to say where they are from or where they were found or can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those 14 persons were exhumed in the area of Bacin but have not been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those 14 persons, are they included in the total of 49 autopsied?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those 49 autopsied have names and surname. 44 from the list we got from the list of the Prosecution, five outside that number but also from Bacin. That's what makes 49. And 14 remain unidentified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another question regarding the site in Bacin. On the list we have 108 persons, 49 autopsied. Can you tell us about the remaining persons from 49 to 108? Are they on the list of missing persons or on the list of dead?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the list are on the list of missing persons, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the document concerning Bruska, the 21st of December, 1991, is the date of disappearance of the people, and the exhumation was on the 26th of April, 1996. The last digits of the number are 695. It is said in this document that another person was autopsied from Bruska, Josip Marinovic, gone missing on the 10th of June, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Trauma is indicated as the cause of death, contusion and bursts in the chest. How did you come to this conclusion? Is there background material?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the record with me but those are details I copied from the autopsy report as drafted by the doctor who performed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Those were all the questions I had about the documents. I would like to know one more thing. Testifying in the Milosevic case in 2003, you spoke about a certain number of exhumed bodies related to Operations Flash and Storm, if I remember correctly. Can you tell us how many persons were concerned then in 2003?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can give the information I know, it's 499 persons from the area of Knin, 300 Gracac, 154 Korenica 27 [as interpreted], and Zvanusa 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to which of the exhumed bodies are related to Flash operation and which to Storm operation, or, rather, how many are related to each of the operations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit I don't have the exact numbers. As far as I know, all that I have just stated is related to the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. Those were all the questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have completed our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, maybe one question concerning the identifications. When you examined remains from mass graves, given the long time between the death of the persons and the examination, did you encounter normal or special problems in -- for identification? Could you give us an overall picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me to take a couple of minutes to explain to you how this service is organised and how the service operates, the one that deals with mortal remains, on the area of Croatia, from those regions from which people went missing, lists of missing persons were made. That was very important, precisely because later it was on the basis of those lists that we were able to look for those people. As soon as the lists were made, we started gathering so-called anti-mortal data that later helped us with identification. We interviewed the closest family and relatives, gathering the details that could be important for identification such as clothing, personal appearance, prior illnesses and conditions, any kind of detail that could be identifying. And on the basis of that information, we compiled the database about missing persons. When the graves became accessible and when exhumations began, we referred to the data collected before so soon a grave was exhumed we started comparing with the database. We already had some potential candidates. We were able to narrow down the possibilities, and many people were identified thanks to the information gathered before, the ante-mortal data that we had stored from before. We were able to identify almost 80 per cent in this way using traditional methods comparing these two parameters. In those cases where such identification was impossible, later on starting with 1996 and onwards, the DNA method was used to solve more complicated cases. However, there are some cases that are simply impossible, primarily those where the bodies have been completely incinerated, mainly in houses where the fire lasted for a long time and the fragments of human bones were so small that they were only identifiable as human bones but could not be used for identification. In such cases when even DNA cannot help because it cannot be isolated from such a bone fragment, the only possibility that remains is to try to reconstruct through witnesses how many people could have been in the house when it burned down, and based on witness statements we can make some inferences about -- inferences about the names and identities. Sometimes bodies were found in wells, in pits, in deep and narrow sites where the remains had spent many years in humidity or in water. The bones were completely destroyed and identification was very difficult, made even more difficult by the fact that all the bones were jumbled. This is where DNA can be very helpful, because based on every -- every fragment, every -- everything that is susceptible to DNA analysis, we can arrive at the exact number of bodies and at -- and give them names. So there is a whole spectrum from the simple cases where we are able to identify then and there on the site who it was, especially when there are only one or two bodies in a grave, to the most complicated cases, the impossible cases where even the latest technology we have today does not help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Doctor, in relation to firearm wounds, you spoke of gunpowder burns -- or, rather, you spoke of burns on the skin and on clothing. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you spoke of relative proximity after telling us about point-blank range. Now, this relative proximity, what distance would it be in metres? What range in metres?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, when we speak of relative proximity, we mean distances from several centimetres to one or one and a half metres depending on the type of firearm and the charge itself, because not the same -- different guns will fire the charge in a different way and the flame will be different. But what we mean by relative proximity goes from several centimetres to one or one and a half metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would that mean that when you say "at a distance," it would be in excess of one and a half metres, or would it depend again on the type of firearm?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It also depends on the type of firearm. But when we say "distance," we mean the kind of distance that leaves no more gunpowder burns, no burns at all, which is more than one and a half metre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, thank you so much. Thank you for coming to testify. We've come to the end of your testimony now. You are excused, and once again thank you for coming. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's time for the break and it actually works out perfectly. We'll have our next witness here ready to testify at quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. The Court will take a short break and come back at quarter to eleven. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I noticed there was a distortion, but I don't see PS on the monitor. There was a face distortion, but are we in private session? Okay. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we are in private session, Your Honour. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But the face distortion is on. Thank you for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, good morning. You were granted certain protective measures, which means you will be referred to by your pseudonym, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? You don't want us to go into private session for this introduction?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary. I will go into private session for the background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You will be referred to by either your pseudonym or just by the word "Witness." You were also granted facial distortion, which means that your face will be distorted in any broadcast of public portion of these proceedings. Do you understand what I said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the assistance -- with the assistance of

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the assistance -- with the assistance of the usher, I would like to show you a piece of paper. Please look at this paper. Do not read it aloud, and confirm whether it is your name, date of birth, and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this sheet into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document indicating the witness's name and date of birth is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 379, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to refer to the map, to the atlas, which is Exhibit 23, and Bosanski Novi can be found on the page 21, grid C3. This is in the right bottom corner of that grid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you very briefly tell the Judges what was the ethnic composition of the municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi had about 40.000 inhabitants. 60 per cent were Serbs, 34 were Bosniaks, Muslims, at the time. The rest were Yugoslavs and others. And there were 1 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Within the municipality, were the villages and town mixed or were there areas that were specifically Bosniaks or specifically Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: The villages were mostly of one ethnicity. The town was roughly 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before 1990, what was the relationship between various ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Very solid. There were no incidents or problems on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did people of various ethnicities socialise, let's say within -- in villages which were just mono-ethnic with villages of people of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: In the villages a little less, but in the town there were a lot of mixed marriages, so you didn't know who was what. In villages they would socialise a little less. They were more closed environments than towns.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the atmosphere changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes. When the war in Croatia broke out, yes, things did change. And during the negotiations while the presidents of the republics discussed the status of Yugoslavia and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell he is what changes were those in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, the mono-ethnic environments and villages closed themselves off more and more. Some barricades were erected. There were village watches, and people contacted less with each other and amongst each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go for a second into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, what were the results of the elections in the municipality of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: The SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, won about 60 per cent of the votes, the Party of Democratic Action 28, and the rest, there was one deputy which was the league of -- the Youth Alliance and the Liberals. There were some of the reformists of Ante Markovic and the former League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you describe the work of the Assembly? We can -- we heard that the SDS party got 60 per cent, SDA got about 28 per cent. How was the work of the party? Was there a cooperation or were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: At the beginning it was quite good cooperation, because the agreement was that the SDS and SDA should divide up power and authority, and where the SDS this 30 per cent of seats in some other municipalities would be given certain positions in executive power, and that's what happened in Bosanski Novi where we were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to approach the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the beginning, everything functioned very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Is it possible for you to move slightly forward towards the microphone? We understand the problem that you have, Witness, but if there is a possibility just to move slightly and bring the microphone closer to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this will be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As you said, at the beginning everything functioned very well. Did there come a time when it didn't work or didn't function very well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, the problems started when the war in Croatia broke out, specifically when the army attacked Hrvatska Kostajnica and several Croatian villages, but that was in Croatia. There's just a river dividing the border between Bosnia and Croatia, the River Una. And that's when certain problems started to arise. Towards the end of 1991, everybody, all the Bosniaks who were in leadership posts were replaced with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You -- just to clarify one thing, you mentioned that army attack Hrvatska Kostajnica. Can you tell us which army do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: It was called the Yugoslav People's Army at the time, but how far it was Yugoslav is a debatable point, because when the war broke out in Slovenia with other ethnic groups, they didn't want to let the army and especially officers. When the war broke out in Croatia, 90 per cent of that army was a Serb army because the new recruits ceased to go to the army, and their places were filled with reservists who mostly came from Serbia. And among others, that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Going back to the work of the Assembly, were there any proposals made by SDS which would be for you, for the SDA, or other parties unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, the first problems began when there was new regionalisation afoot in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDS endeavoured to have all Serb majority municipalities form one region. That was something we'd already seen in Croatia. When they separated from Croatia there was a compact territory which they defended by force of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say that they separated from Croatia and they defended by force of arms, can you be specific again? Which regions do you have in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Slavonia, part of Slavonia, and the whole of the area around Knin along the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, along that border belt. So Zagreb and Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were completely separated geographically because those were places where the Serbs were in the majority, and with the help of the army they cleansed the region of Croats and it became a compact hole. Knin, Hrvatska Kostajnica, Dvor is characteristic for Bosanski Novi because we're only divided by a river there. Two towns on the banks of the same river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this region called -- I'm sorry. I will rephrase my question. Was there any name for this region which was separated from the rest of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: It was -- they called it Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that SDS in Bosanski Novi, there was this issue of regionalisation in Bosanski Novi. What exactly they wanted to achieve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, before the war Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say during communism, it had six regions, Yugoslav -- some of the municipalities in the Bihac area, municipality where there was a Serb majority, they endeavoured to join on to the Banja Luka region where they were in power in the municipality to create a region there, the aim of which -- well, we saw what the aim of that was later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can you -- can you again be more specific and say what the aim was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, their aim, they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia at all costs. That was part of the territory where they had created -- where the army had come, where they took over power, where they had absolute power, and from where they managed their war operations. In the other Serb municipalities there wasn't a Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Going back to the work of the Assembly and politicians, can you tell us briefly who were the major politicians on the SDS side and then on the SDA side? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, specifically in the SDS the alpha and omega of that was Gavro Bogic. After him you had Radovan Pasic, Umbaro Dami [phoen], Domazet [phoen] Nikola, Dejanovic, Nazalac [phoen], Nikola Graunic [phoen]. That was the sort of elite from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in the SDA who were the major --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: In the SDA the president was Hamed Agic, I think he was the number one man. Resad Berberovic, Dzafer Kapetanovic, Arim Bajrektarevic back and so on. Izet Musemuvic [phoen], Hasim Valjevac, and that was expanded with the Main Board later on and the Presidencies of the branch offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mention this Gavro Bogic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Gavro Bogic was a deputy in the state Assembly. I think he was an economist by profession, and he was the director general of a firm called Jadra [sic]. Before that I think he was the managing director in Lignosper, but before the war he was the director general of the Japra firm, which is a firm dealing in mining and construction engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that Gavro Bogic was the alpha and omega in the municipality. In which way? Can you specify what you meant stating that he was alpha and omega?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Mostly you had to ask him about everything. Pasic Radovan was a relatively young man and he wasn't in the League of Communists, so this was someone new, but Gavro Bogic managed everything. Whenever a problem cropped up in the Assembly, for instance, he had the final say, and his proposals were accepted by the SDS, and in inter-party agreements, whenever any problems arose he would settle them and decide the way he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mention this Pasic. Who was Radomir Pasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Radomir Pasic was a lawyer. He had graduated in law. He was born in 1964. He was a young man of 28 at the time. For a time he worked as a lawyer in a department store called Jedinstvo. He was a young man without a pedigree in the League of Communists, and I think that's why he came to be the president of the SDS. And later on he was president of the Crisis Staff in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did he have also a position in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, he was the mayor. It wasn't referred to as mayor, but that's what he was, the mayor of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to talk a little bit about propaganda. After the war started in Croatia, were you aware of any propaganda speeches on either side, on the side of Serbs or on the side of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, on the Serb side all their journalists, everybody joined in the system, and they started invoking the past where a million Serbs were killed in Jasenovac. They talked about the Ustasha authorities. They were afraid that that would happen again. And in Bosanski Novi, Bera Dragan was a journalist himself and he was very prominent in things like that. He presented various lies in order to create this sort of fear amongst the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any programme -- we're receiving B/C/S interpretation. I think it's now -- were there any programmes on radio that caused -- caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: The morning broadcast, but Bera Dragan was the host and he would begin by saying, "Good morning, Kraj -- people of the Krajin -- the Krajisnici," and he thought -- he spoke about the unification of all Serb lands and so on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he just said, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, the interpreter didn't catch what you said. Can you repeat it after what you said that, that this Bera Dragan had programme in which he always -- he began by saying, "Good morning, people of the Krajisnici"? What did you say after that? "He spoke about the unification of all Serb lands," and ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: There were a lot of rumours amongst the people that this sort of unification of some Serb lands was being proposed and that was where the krajinas in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia, that area. And at the time the overall Croatian Krajina was cleansed of all other ethnic groups except for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this issue ever discussed at the Municipal Assembly, the possibilities of these two krajinas to be joined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of discussion when they tried to impose this new regionalisation, and everybody put forward their arguments for and against. What they needed was a decision, a two-third majority decision which they did not have. They were only able to implement the decision by exerting pressure on Mladen, the youth representative. They threatened his father saying they would set fire to his motel and throw explosives on it. So he voted in favour. So there was a lot of comment of this type going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were still in -- in Bosanski Novi, was there any progress in relation to this proposal of joining those two krajinas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, that was functioning to a great extent. On the military plain it was going ahead full speed. The Serbs responded to the mobilisation call in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were sent to Hrvatska Grubica [as interpreted]. And on the economic and political plain, well, the economy was so bad that it wasn't important any more. It was the military aspect that game to the fore and that was functioning properly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking about army, were there any armed formation which would come to -- to the municipality of Bosanski Novi from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes, specifically the cleansing of Muslims along the Japra River valley, units from Kninva and Dvor Na Uni which is on Croatian territory. They crossed over and helped the Serbs to expel the people and all the agricultural machinery, tractors and everything were taken away and property taken, seized. Now, before that tomorrow people crossed over in uniforms they kidnapped people in Bosanski Novi, the Bosniaks. They would take them away. Some people went missing without a trace. Some were returned but interrogated and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have to take this little bit step-by-step. You said that someone cross the bridge. People were kidnap. Who -- who are you talking about? Who were these people who crossed the bridge and did call kind of things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: From Bosanski Novi in those elite units of theirs they were called Specials, but I think these were in their militia, the police of Krajina. Some well-known criminals went there; they were given weapons quite simply. They were recruited over there. And in Bosanski Novi they caused a great deal of problems with their weapons. They threw hand grenades of cafes owned by Albanians and Muslims. For example, Hodzic, I don't know his first name, but he worked in the legal department of Bosanski Novi. He was a lawyer, and he put a pistol to their -- to his back. He was taken across the bridge. He was interrogated, beaten up, subjected to torture by electrical shock. And another man, Dedic, was also taken away. He was fishing in the river, but he was taken across the river and nothing is none of him to the present day. Mehmed Hamzagic was another example. For a time he was beaten up and subjected to electrical shock torture and interrogated. He didn't know anything. For a time he was released, but several days later he also disappeared without a trace. So that was still when there was peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all these things going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, at the beginning you mentioned that this -- there was an elite unit called Specials. Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, they came from Dvor. They were accommodated there, which is in Krajina, in Croatia, and the place is called Dvor. And when they had accomplished their assignments, they would go back there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said they were called Specialists. Do you know who did they belong to, under which unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Specifically, I don't know the name of the unit because the insignia were changed. Instead of the five-pointed star there was the two-headed eagle, and I think on some of their patches it said, "Militia," "Milicija," or, "Police of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whom they were subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, I think that at the time the policing Krajina was controlled by Milan Martic. He was the minister of the police, and I think that he was in charge of that overall part of the army and some officers who came from Belgrade but had different names to cover up. So it didn't appear to be an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also said that from the territory of Bosanski Novi there were people who joined this -- this unit of Specialist. How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, they would go back with those uniforms, and they said that they had -- the power was in their hands. They would brag about it. Some people were patriots, patriot Serbs that it did it because of that, but others were criminals and they engaged in petty theft, violence, and so on. I know those people generally by their nicknames. I think that there was a man who was in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't catch the nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he appeared one day wearing a uniform. There was Grga, there was Brk, names like that. They were all people who otherwise were criminals and where legal proceedings had been taken against them and they were in prison. So Grk, Titin those were some of the nicknames, and Grga.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you mean before they joined this unit they were in prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did they work together with these units coming from -- from Dvor Na Uni or from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes. And nobody prevented them from crossing the bridge in their spare time with their weapons. And then they would just instil a reign of terror and destroy cafes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us these units coming -- which were coming from Croatian side, what kinds of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: All of them wore the olive-grey uniforms of the former JNA and new camouflage uniforms as well, camouflage military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they had in possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Automatic rifles mostly, automatic weapons. Rifles manufactured in Kragujevac of the type that the former JNA had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking about their behaviour, you already stated that they arrested few people, and you explained that they were beaten, tortured. Where did they take them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: To Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know approximately for how long they kept them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Up to seven days. Five, six days, seven days, depending.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mention that they destroyed cafes. Apart from cafes -- first, in which way they destroyed these cafes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: They would throw hand grenades most often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they target just the cafes or some other properties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, usually they would pick cafes or small restaurants. I was an eyewitness in the case of a cafe called Maksuti owned by an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did local police take any actions, prevent crimes committed by these formations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: At the beginning while late Djuro Umicevic, chief of police, was still alive they did what they could, however, the powers of the police were very limited. All of the villages had been armed for a while. The Serb villages had organised themselves, and the police had no power to do much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mention that Milan Martic, at least what you knew, was minister of police. Do you know whether or not Milan Martic ever come to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes. I personally saw him on two or thorough cases in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were these locations? What were the circumstances you saw him in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Once there were rallies being held when he came, and once I saw him with the top leadership of the SDS on a visit, and I saw him once with a man who was a butcher. I don't know him. But I know him only as the man who rented his cafe to a football club. He later proclaimed himself to be a Chetnik leader, vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these were the occasions you saw Milan Martic in Bosanski Novi. Did you -- did you see some other politician -- politicians from other parts of former Yugoslavia coming to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Well, some lower-ranking politicians came from Serbia. Brdjanin from Banja Luka and others from the Regional Board of the SDS. Karadzic came once, Krajisnik, and from the top leadership of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some from the SDS leaders of the Serbian Krajina, including the late Raskovic who established the SDS in Croatia. He visited Bosanski Novi once.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Vojislav Seselj ever visited Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the occasion he visited it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: I think on the occasion of the big rally that was held in the park, the city park in Bosanski Novi. That rally was in support of the Serbs in Krajina, because war was by that time raging in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go previously into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you return to the municipality? You don't need to be specific about the places which you visited. I just want to know whether you return.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: When I was in Bosanska Krupa, after that I returned, I stayed until the 24th of February and went to Zagreb. And after the war, I came back again in 1998, because that was a time when it was possible to come on a visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When -- when you return, how did you find the Bosnian places, the places occupied before by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: It was a catastrophe. Everything was grown over. Everything was like a desert. Maybe in Blagaj there were four or five houses left standing. Everything else was destroyed, roofs torn off, overgrown by weed, woods, brush. You couldn't recognise the places even if you were born around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My last question: Do you know anything about the fate of SDA activists from 1991, 1992, for example Dzafer Kapetanovic or Resad Berberovic? What happened to these major SDA players in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-046
utterances.text: All of them were arrested and detained, people from the Main Board, many activists including those you enumerated. All of them were locked up at the camp, at the stadium, and they never got out. They were seen to be beaten and interrogated about things they couldn't have any clue about. They asked them about rockets and such things that we had never seen or even heard about their existence. Many of them were taken by truck one day to Radusica Potok, as some say, and nobody ever heard of them again. Some were found later in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the cross-examination will be led by my co-counsel, Mr. Nikola Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perovic. Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin the cross-examination, may I suggest that the usher distribute what I have in my hands. I have sufficient copies of the witness's statement in the English language, the interview he gave to OTP investigators, because practically all my questions will relate to that statement. And I have another suggestion, that we continue to work in private session out of an abundance of caution in view of the protective measures enjoyed by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely understand Defence counsel's difficulty. However, I do notice that on the 24th of April it does not appear that there are any trials that are sitting in the afternoon. So perhaps we could accommodate the Defence counsel if we simply moved into the afternoon session on Monday, the 24th, and that would give Defence counsel time to get back on Monday morning, which is apparently what he thought was going to happen. If that presents a difficulty, I'm not -- I'm willing to go along with any other arrangements that are suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, what I don't understand is that when we talked about this break, and we thought we would come back to work on the 20th -- I beg your pardon, on the 18th, you stood up to say, no, no, no, but this is Orthodox Easter so we need the rest of the week, and we gave away the four days of the rest of the week because we were trying to accommodate the Orthodox Easter. Now the Orthodox Easter moves further on beyond the 18th to the 21st. It moves into now the 23rd. How does this come about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. It was my mistake. Good Friday is on the 18th. Sunday is on the -- Easter is on Sunday. And that is why I thought you said, as you did indeed, that we would reconvene on Monday, but I forgot that this meant that we should leave on Sunday morning to be here on Monday. So I omitted to say that. It was my mistake. I will -- I won't insist, but it would be important because it's an important holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it be okay if we sat in the afternoon on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't say exactly now because I don't know the transportation problems. Well, I'd rather have the schedule as it stands rather than being bound to come here on Monday afternoon. I can't take that risk, say that I will appear on Monday afternoon and then not appear. That would be quite improper. But it's something out of my control depending on transport facilities, and so on and so forth, traffic and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milovancevic, you have booked your ticket. You now know which flight you are flying on back from the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We have reserved our departure flights. We still have to reserve our return flights via the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you -- how does this affect your scheduling of witnesses? Are you able to accommodate Mr. Milovancevic if we don't sit at all on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. We will just move the witness who was going to be on the 24th a little bit later in the week. So we can certainly accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will then not sit at all on Monday, the 24th. We will start on the 25th. Having said that, I must say I give this day very grudgingly. This is now the fifth day, if you add it to the four days of the previous week. Somehow we must try and make means to cover these days. I don't know how, but I think we must try and do that when we come back. Okay? There is an issue. If that is all that was going to be raised by the parties, the Chamber has something to raise, and seeing that we will not come back for the afternoon session, maybe we might as well deal with this. There are a number of documents which have been marked for identification, and they are getting quite a many. Let me just sort of go through them. There were two documents introduced during Mr. Theunens which were MFIs 112 and 113. Then there was a document introduced during the testimony of Maksic, which is MFI 131. And there were 11 documents introduced during the testimony of Mr. Babic, MFIs 200, 201, 202, 223, 225, 226, 227, 228, 2231 -- I beg your pardon, 231, 233, and 241. Now, as regards the MFI 112 and 113 -- well, 113, if I don't -- if I'm not mistaken, there was no request that it be tendered into evidence, and I think whoever was responsible should decide whether it will be tendered or not. But let me talk about MFI 112 and 131. They were tendered for admission by the Defence and the Prosecution respectively and they were marked for identification as a result of the opposing party's objection to the admissibility. MFI 112 is an UNPROFOR document object contained in the book entitled western Slavonia May 1995 exodus, and this document was tendered by the Defence during cross-examination. The Prosecution did not object to admission of the document itself on the condition that the title of the document, which was seemingly added by the author of the book, is not regarded as part of the evidence.
